title: Equilibrium and the First Law
short: Zero net force means constant velocity, and standing still is the special case where that velocity is zero.
trouble: Students think an object moving at constant speed needs a net force in its direction of motion.

blocks.html: Newton's First Law: Inertia said an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts. With Free-Body Diagrams, that becomes a tool: whenever the velocity is constant, the forces on the diagram must add to zero.

Equilibrium means $\Sigma \vec{F} = 0$, which happens exactly when the velocity is constant: at rest, or moving in a straight line at a steady speed. In components: $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$.

A net force changes velocity; that is what the second law says. So if the velocity isn't changing, there is no net force, whatever the speed. A car cruising at $30\ \text{m/s}$ on a straight road is in equilibrium just as much as a parked car: the forward force from the road exactly balances drag and rolling friction.

blocks.name: ph-dynamics

opts.task: Set the push equal to the friction force (μ_k mg = 5.9 N here, so try about 6 N). Once the cart is moving, it keeps a steady speed.

blocks.cap: A pushed cart with friction. Balanced forces keep its speed steady; they don't stop it.

items: If the object is at rest or moves at a steady velocity, write $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$.
Solve for the unknown force; the speed itself never appears.

blocks.title: Constant velocity
blocks.q: You push a $40\ \text{kg}$ crate across a floor at a constant velocity with a $120\ \text{N}$ horizontal push. How big is the friction force?
steps: $120 - f = 0$, so $f = 120\ \text{N}$. The mass isn't needed.

blocks.title: Moving, yet balanced
blocks.q: An elevator car of mass $800\ \text{kg}$ rises at a steady $2\ \text{m/s}$. What is the cable's tension?
steps: $T = (800)(9.8) = 7{,}840\ \text{N}$, the same as if it were parked.

blocks.html: Thinking an object moving at a constant speed needs a net force in its direction of motion. That idea fits everyday life, where friction stops things, but the extra push only cancels friction. Check: is the velocity changing? If not, the net force is zero, and the forward forces equal the backward ones.
Try it in the Science Lab: The First Law: Inertia.
